title: Diego Maradona
wiki_lead:
Diego Armando Maradona (30 October 1960 – 25 November 2020) was an Argentine professional football player and manager. Widely regarded as one of the greatest players of all time, he was an attacking midfielder renowned for his exceptional creativity, vision, passing, ball control, dribbling, and free-kick taking. A predominantly left-footed playmaker, he could also operate as a second striker. Nicknamed El Pibe de Oro ("The Golden Boy"), he was named one of the two winners of the FIFA Player of the Century award in 2000, alongside Pelé.
Born in Lanús and raised in Villa Fiorito, a villa miseria on the outskirts of Buenos Aires, Maradona began his professional career with Argentinos Juniors in 1976, making his debut at the age of 15. He joined Boca Juniors in 1981 and helped the club win the 1981 Metropolitano championship. In 1982, he moved to Barcelona for a [[List of most expensive association football transfers
|world-record transfer fee]], winning the Copa del Rey and Copa de la Liga in 1983. He transferred to Napoli in 1984, breaking his own world transfer record. During his seven seasons in Italy, Maradona transformed Napoli into a major force in Italian and European football, leading the club to its first two Serie A titles, in 1987 and 1990, as well as the Coppa Italia in 1987, the 1988–89 UEFA Cup and the Supercoppa Italiana in 1990. He later played for Sevilla and Newell's Old Boys before returning to Boca Juniors, where he retired in 1997.
At international level, Maradona made 91 appearances and scored 34 goals for Argentina between 1977 and 1994. After leading Argentina to the 1979 FIFA World Youth Championship title, he captained the senior team to victory at the 1986 World Cup in Mexico, scoring five goals, providing five assists and winning the Golden Ball as the tournament's best player. In the quarter-final against England, he scored both goals in a 2–1 victory. The first, known as the "Hand of God", was scored illegally with his hand, while the second followed a solo run from inside his own half and was later voted the "Goal of the Century". He also scored both goals in the semi-final against Belgium and set up Jorge Burruchaga's winning goal against West Germany in the final. Maradona captained Argentina again at the 1990 World Cup, where they lost in the final. He went on to win the 1993 Artemio Franchi Cup, his last title.
Maradona struggled with drug addiction during his playing career. He received a 15-month suspension in 1991 after testing positive for cocaine and was excluded from the 1994 FIFA World Cup after testing positive for ephedrine. As a manager, he coached the Argentina national team from 2008 to 2010 and led them to the quarter-finals of the 2010 World Cup. He also managed clubs in the United Arab Emirates, Mexico and Argentina, ending his managerial career with Gimnasia de La Plata in 2020. Beyond his sporting achievements, Maradona became a cultural icon, particularly in Argentina and Naples; his popularity inspired religious devotion among some supporters, reflected in shrines and religious imagery dedicated to him. After his death in 2020, Argentina declared three days of national mourning, and Napoli's home stadium was renamed Stadio Diego Armando Maradona in his honour.

Early life
Maradona was born on 30 October 1960, at the Policlínico Evita Hospital in Lanús, Buenos Aires Province, to a poor Roman Catholic family. He was raised in Villa Fiorito, a shantytown on the southern outskirts of Buenos Aires. His father, also named Diego Maradona, worked at a chemicals factory. His mother, Dalma Salvadora Franco, was of Italian and Croatian descent. Maradona's parents grew up in Esquina in the north-east province of Corrientes, and moved to Buenos Aires in the 1950s. Maradona's two younger brothers, Hugo and Raúl, both became professional footballers. He also had four older sisters.

Maradona captained Argentina to victory in the 1986 FIFA World Cup in Mexico, playing every minute and contributing five goals and five assists, including the quarter-final goals against England: the first a deliberate handball he later dubbed the " Hand of God," and the second a mesmerizing 60-yard solo dribble past five defenders known as the " Goal of the Century." He earned the Golden Ball as the tournament's best player despite the controversies surrounding his methods.
